Appendix 9
APPENDIX 9
KORBANOS
FAQ: Really? Am I supposed to wake up each morning 
(and on Rosh Chodesh and Yom Tov) and say to myself: 
“I sooo wish I could go bring an animal sacrifice this 
morning”? How are we supposed to relate to a concept 
that seems to be so foreign to us?
First, let’s get rid of some misconceptions. The word “

” does not translate as “sacrifice” (as in giving something up), even though in English we seem to use the term “animal sacrifices.” It also does not translate as “offering,” as in bringing a gift or bribe to the angry gods, as it is in the way we view
help a person get closer to Hashem. When we had a Beis Hamikdash, we took the animal parts, and by placing them on the

(Altar), they became elevated. This is a personal declaration of our intentions to elevate all the material stuff that Hashem gave us (our physical powers, emotional skills, possessions 
— 
whatever Hashem gave 
us) to a higher level, to direct it all toward serving Hashem and accomplishing our mission here on earth. In addition, the blood of the animal sprinkled on the

serves as a reminder of our vulnerability. This “near-death” type of experience is meant to motivate us to continue growing spiritually and getting as close to Hashem as humanly possible while we’re still on this earth — which is not forever!To emphasize the point that
are to bring us closer to Hashem rather than to “appease an angry god,” it is interesting to note that the name of Hashem used in connection with

is specifically His four-letter name that we do not pronounce, which is His attribute of love and mercy. The name Elokim (which represents His trait of strict judgment) only appears five times in the whole of
, and always in the context of other nations, not Bnei Yisrael!
